messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maria was twenty‑six, a first‑year biology major at a midsize university, and the daughter of a single mother who works nights as a nurse. She spent most of her week in the campus chemistry lab, where she was supposed to be conducting a harmless experiment on ethanol vapor. One humid Thursday afternoon, the hood failed to seal properly, and a spray of a toxic solvent filled the small, dimly lit workspace. Maria felt a searing sting on her skin, the air thickened, and she collapsed. When she awoke hours later, her body was a raw, aching mess, and the smell of antiseptic lingered in her memory of the event. The darkness of the lab, the suddenness of the chemical spray, and the way the emergency lights flickered became the first anchors of her distress. Those dark, dim spaces would later set off a cascade of reactions that she could not stop. In the weeks that followed, every encounter with a dark hallway on campus, every quiet night while she studied in the library’s rarely used wing, and every whiff of disinfectant in the university health clinic would make her heart pound and her hands tremble. The darkness itself triggered her to avoid every dimly lit room and to stay in the brightly lit portion of the campus. That avoidance—her deliberate avoidance of the very spaces that had once contained danger—became a core maladaptive strategy. The same darkness also triggered a threat response: she would startle at the slightest touch, her muscles would tense, and she could not help but feel that the chemical’s remnants were still there. Moreover, the sight of night-time on the campus map pulled her memories back to the moment the hood failed; the smell of antiseptic would surface memories she could not fully name. All these triggers set the stage for her next set of reactions. Maria’s self‑appraisal had become a harsh inner critic. She began to tell herself that something was wrong with her, that her body was a traitor, and that she could no longer trust what her senses felt. Those negative appraisals fed into her avoidance. Knowing she was defective, she thought, “If I stay in the dark, I might lose control again.” That conviction tightened her resolve to erase the memory of the accident whenever it surfaced. Each time she tried to clear her mind, the memory returned more vividly, causing her body to ache in the same painful spots as during the exposure. The pain recall and the confused sequence of events—her inability to put the exact order of the spill, the shudder, the collapse—only reinforced her belief that she was defective. The memory’s persistence, in turn, triggered even more negative appraisals. The more she struggled to name the event, the more convinced she became that she was a flawed person whose body could not be trusted. In a cruel feedback loop, the memory and the negative appraisal amplified one another, and each time the memory surfaced it made the dark spaces even more threatening, while the negative appraisal intensified her fear of darkness, reinforcing the original triggers. The threat reactions that followed each trigger—startle responses, muscle tension, the feeling of being on guard—became a secondary strategy to keep her safe. Every time she felt the body’s alarm surge, she would scan her surroundings for signs of danger, checking for chemical spills in the lab, or the presence of anyone who might touch her unexpectedly. These checks became constant, a way of proving to herself that she was still in control. Yet each check, in its own way, reminded her of the event; the physical act of checking was a painful reminder of the chemical on her skin, and the sense that she had to keep her body on alert felt like a threat to her bodily integrity. The threat responses reinforced her avoidance, keeping her away from the very rooms where she could learn, thus harming her academic progress and further isolating her. Maria’s avoidance behaviors had concrete consequences. She began skipping the chemistry lab sessions, citing “the lab’s lights flickering,” and she avoided the library’s low‑light reading corners, which left her feeling socially disconnected. She started to dread going to the campus health clinic, where the antiseptic smell was almost omnipresent. As her grades slipped, the guilt and shame increased, feeding her negative appraisals and her sense of personal failure. She began to feel that she could not trust her own body to keep her safe, that she was fundamentally defective, and that the only way to survive was to erase the memory, to avoid the triggers, and to check every environment for threats. These strategies, while temporarily protective, only amplified the very threat feelings they were meant to reduce. It was the night she missed a group presentation because she could not bring herself into the lecture hall’s dimly lit auditorium that pushed her to seek help. She had never been a social person, but the idea of losing the opportunity to complete her coursework and the looming fear that she might never again trust her own body or her senses made her decide to talk to a counselor. She is now hoping that someone can help her untangle the loop that keeps her body on alert, that she can relearn the names of her own sensations, and that she can learn to trust the dark spaces of her campus again. The most frightening thought that keeps her awake at night is that the accident will forever dictate how she moves through the world—until she can break the cycle.
